name: Shungite Pyramid
subtitle: Shungite, 8cm x 8cm pyramid
standfirst: A pyramid cut and polished from shungite, the carbon-bearing stone from the shungite deposits of Karelia in north west Russia. This is a mineral object, not a food supplement: no dose, no ingredients list, just the stone itself, 8cm at the base.
body: Shungite comes from a group of deposits in Karelia, in north west Russia, close to Lake Onega. The rock formed in the Precambrian, somewhere around two billion years ago, from organic sediment that was buried, heated and compressed until its carbon content locked into place. It is one of the oldest carbon-bearing rocks known, and one of the few places on earth where carbon of this kind occurs in a solid, workable stone rather than as coal or graphite.

The stone itself is black, dense and slightly greasy to the touch when polished, closer in feel to graphite than to a typical crystal. It cuts and takes a shine well, which is why it is worked into pyramids, spheres and jewellery rather than left as raw rubble. This piece is cut to an 8cm x 8cm pyramid, with the four faces polished to a low sheen.

Shungite is also one of the very few natural minerals known to contain fullerenes, carbon molecules including C60, in trace amounts. That is a genuine, documented feature of the rock's chemistry. It is a fact about what the stone is made of, not a description of anything it does once it is in a room.
spec: Karelia, north west Russia, near Lake Onega
Precambrian, estimated at around two billion years old
Contains naturally occurring fullerenes, including C60, in trace amounts
dose: Not applicable. This is a mineral object, not a food supplement, and is not taken by mouth.
cautions: Not a food supplement and not for ingestion.
Keep away from small children: a stone this size and weight is a choking and impact hazard.
Polished stone can chip if dropped on a hard surface, handle it the way you would any dense mineral piece.
imageSubject: A black polished shungite pyramid, 8cm at the base, photographed against a plain neutral surface, showing its dark lustre.
queries: No weight is given for this pyramid on the current listing. Can Reiss supply it so the spec sheet is complete.

The live listing doesn't state a carbon grade or percentage for this pyramid, unlike the Elite Noble Shungite Stone (99%) or the Water Stones (99%). Is this the same high-carbon grade, or the more common lower-carbon shungite typically used for larger carved pieces? That single fact would materially change what we can say about it.

Removed claim: the live listing says this pyramid neutralises EMF radiation from WiFi, phones and 3G, 4G and 5G signals. This is an unevidenced product claim and would fail an ASA assessment. It has been removed entirely and does not appear anywhere on the rebuilt page.

Removed claim: the live listing describes the stone as providing antioxidant support, restoring electron balance, protecting cells and reducing oxidative stress, and enhancing wellbeing. All of this has been removed as unauthorised health claim language.

name: Lion's Mane
subtitle: Hericium erinaceus, vegan capsules
standfirst: Hericium erinaceus, the shaggy white bracket fungus known as lion's mane, encapsulated on its own with no fillers. The listing doesn't yet print a capsule count, a capsule weight or an extraction method, so this page states only what is confirmed and queries the rest.
body: Hericium erinaceus grows on the wounds of hardwood trees, mostly beech and oak, in temperate forests across the northern hemisphere. It fruits as a single cascading mass of long white spines rather than a cap and stem, which is where its common names come from: lion's mane, bearded tooth, monkey head, pom pom mushroom.

Herbase's capsules are described on the listing as 100% Hericium erinaceus with no fillers, bulking agents or contaminants. What isn't stated is whether the mushroom used is fruiting body, grown on logs or substrate and harvested as the actual fungus, or mycelium grown on grain, which is a cheaper and very different material sold under the same name. Neither is disclosed on the current listing, and it's the single most useful thing this label could say.

The same goes for extraction. A capsule can be filled with plain dried powder, or with a hot water or dual extract concentrated to a stated ratio, and the two behave very differently. None of that is printed here either. A beta-glucan percentage, the marker most labels use to show how much of the mushroom's structural material actually made it into the capsule, is also missing.
spec: Lion's mane, bearded tooth fungus, monkey head mushroom, pom pom mushroom
None stated beyond the capsule shell: described as free from fillers, bulking agents and contaminants
dose: Two capsules in the morning with at least 500 ml of spring water.
supply: Capsule count and capsule weight are not printed on the current listing, so we can't give a day count here. See queries.
cautions: Always consult a healthcare professional before use, particularly if pregnant, nursing or taking medication.
Not suitable for anyone with a known mushroom or fungal allergy.

name: Elite Noble Shungite Stone
subtitle: Noble grade shungite, approx. 20-30 g
standfirst: A hand-sized piece of noble shungite, the high-carbon grade of the stone, cut from the Karelia deposits in north west Russia. Around 20 to 30 grams, no ingredients, no dose: a mineral object described as what it is.
body: Shungite from Karelia varies a great deal by grade. Ordinary shungite runs to somewhere between 30 and 50 percent carbon and is dull black. The rarer grade, sometimes called noble or elite shungite, runs much higher, close to pure carbon, and has a silvery, almost metallic lustre where ordinary shungite is matte. This stone is sold as that higher grade.

The listing states a carbon content of around 99 percent for this stone. That figure describes the proportion of the rock that is carbon, which is a straightforward compositional fact about a mineral, the same kind of figure you'd expect for any ore or gemstone. It is not a description of anything the stone does once you own it.

Shungite of any grade, including this one, is also one of the few natural minerals known to contain trace fullerenes, including C60. That's a genuine feature of the rock's chemistry and worth stating plainly. Each stone weighs approximately 20 to 30 grams, small enough to sit in a pocket or a drawer.
spec: Shungite, noble or elite grade (high carbon content)
Approximately 99%, as stated by the supplier
Precambrian, estimated at around two billion years old
Contains naturally occurring fullerenes, including C60, in trace amounts
dose: Not applicable. This is a mineral object, not a food supplement, and is not taken by mouth.
supply: One stone per order, weighing approximately 20 to 30 g.
cautions: Not a food supplement and not for ingestion.
Keep away from small children: a stone this size is a choking hazard.
imageSubject: A single lustrous, silvery-black noble shungite stone, roughly palm sized, photographed against a plain neutral surface showing its metallic sheen.
queries: Can Reiss confirm a lab assay or certificate for the 99% carbon figure, given it is now the headline compositional fact on this page?

The live listing describes the stone as '99% C60', which conflates carbon content with fullerene content. Fullerenes occur in shungite only in trace amounts, a natural stone cannot be 99% fullerene. We've written the 99% figure as carbon content and mentioned fullerenes separately without a percentage. Worth checking with the supplier which figure the 99% actually refers to.

name: Reishi
subtitle: Ganoderma lucidum, 50 vegan capsules x 800 mg
standfirst: Ganoderma lucidum, sold as reishi, 50 vegan capsules at 800 mg each. Described on the listing as 100% pure with no fillers.
body: Ganoderma lucidum is a bracket fungus that grows on the trunks and roots of deciduous trees, particularly plum, oak and maple. In the wild it forms a hard, woody, kidney-shaped cap with a glossy, varnished-looking surface, dark reddish-brown fading to cream at the growing edge. It is known across East Asia by many names, most commonly reishi in Japan and lingzhi in China, and has one of the longest continuous trade histories of any medicinal mushroom.

Herbase's capsules list the fill as 800 mg of Ganoderma lucidum, described as 100% pure, in a pack of 50 vegan capsules. What the listing doesn't say is whether that 800 mg is the whole mushroom in powdered form, fruiting body or mycelium grown on grain, or a concentrated extract at a stated ratio. It also doesn't give a beta-glucan figure. These are the facts that would tell a customer what grade of reishi they're actually buying, and none of them are on the label yet.
spec: None printed beyond the capsule shell
dose: Two capsules daily with breakfast or lunch, with at least 500 ml of spring water.
supply: Fifty capsules. At two a day that's 25 days.
cautions: Always consult a healthcare professional before use, particularly if pregnant, nursing or taking medication.
Not suitable for anyone with a known mushroom or fungal allergy.

name: Omega Oil
subtitle: Omega-3 oil, 6:1 ratio, 9,000 mg per tablespoon
standfirst: A liquid oil blend formulated to a stated ratio of six parts omega-3 to one part omega-6, delivering 9,000 mg of omega-3 per tablespoon. The listing doesn't name the plant it comes from or confirm the DHA content, so both are logged as queries.
body: The listing describes this oil as rich in alpha-linolenic acid, ALA, an omega-3 fatty acid, blended to a ratio of six parts omega-3 to one part omega-6. It states a figure of 9,000 mg of omega-3 per tablespoon. What it doesn't state anywhere is which plant the oil is pressed from, whether that's flaxseed, hemp, chia or something else, and there's no separate DHA figure printed, only the total omega-3 number.

That distinction matters. ALA is a precursor the body converts into other fatty acids including DHA, but it isn't DHA itself, and a product's DHA content has to be measured and printed on its own to say anything about DHA specifically. Until we have that figure and the source plant confirmed, this page states the ratio and the total omega-3 figure as printed and nothing more.
spec: Not printed on the current listing
Not stated on the current listing
supply: One bottle. Printed on the listing as a one month supply. Bottle volume in millilitres is not given.
cautions: Always consult a healthcare professional before taking supplements.
Not intended to replace prescription medication.
Check the full ingredients and allergen list on the bottle before use.
imageSubject: A spoonful of golden-green oil in natural light, showing its colour and viscosity. No bottle, cap or label.
queries: What plant is this oil pressed from? The listing only says it is rich in ALA and doesn't name a source, flax, hemp, chia or otherwise. This also determines whether the product is vegan, which matters given other Herbase products are marked as such.

Is there a DHA figure in milligrams per serving printed anywhere, separate from the total omega-3 figure? DHA has an authorised claim on the GB Nutrition and Health Claims Register, but only if the product delivers a qualifying amount of DHA specifically and that amount is printed. If Reiss can supply that figure, we can look at whether the authorised wording applies. We have not written that claim here.
What is the bottle size in millilitres?

Given the product doesn't appear to contain preformed DHA, only its precursor ALA, should 'DHA' remain in the product's name at all? We've named it 'Omega Oil' on this page pending an answer, dropping 'DHA' from the name until it's confirmed.

name: Anamu
subtitle: Petiveria alliacea, 50 vegan capsules
standfirst: Petiveria alliacea, sold as Anamu, 50 vegan capsules with no fillers, binders or artificial ingredients.
body: Petiveria alliacea is a shrub native to the Caribbean and South America, also known as guinea hen weed, mucura or tipi. It grows wild across the region and is a familiar plant in Caribbean and South American herbal traditions, most easily identified by the strong sulphurous, garlic-like smell that comes off its crushed leaves and root, a smell that carries through into the dried and encapsulated material.

That smell comes from sulphur compounds in the plant, including dibenzyl trisulphide, one of the compounds Anamu is best known for chemically. Herbase's capsules are 100% Petiveria alliacea, harvested from organically grown sources in the Caribbean and South America, with no fillers, binders or artificial ingredients added at the encapsulation stage.

Each pack is 50 vegan capsules. The listing's own guidance on how long that lasts doesn't agree with itself, at one capsule a day it calls fifty capsules a forty day supply, which is a discrepancy we've flagged rather than repeated here.

body: Inonotus obliquus grows on living birch trees in cold climates across the northern hemisphere, forming a hard, black, cracked mass on the trunk that looks more like burnt charcoal than a mushroom. That black mass, properly called a conk or sclerotium, is the part harvested and used, rather than a cap and gills.

Herbase's capsules list 750 mg of pure Chaga extract per capsule, in a vegan formulation free from fillers or additives. As with the other mushroom pages in this batch, what isn't stated is whether that 750 mg is dried whole material or a concentrated extract at a given ratio, whether it's the conk itself or mycelium grown on grain, and what the beta-glucan content is. The pack doesn't state how many capsules it contains either.

name: Shilajit
subtitle: Altai Mountain resin, 50 g amber glass jar
standfirst: A dual-extracted resin scraped from rock in the Altai Mountains, sold in a 50 g amber glass jar. Fulvic acid and humic acid are named on the listing as compounds present in the resin.
body: Shilajit is a dark, sticky resin that seeps out of rock strata in a handful of high-altitude mountain regions, the Altai among them. It forms over long stretches of time as plant matter, trapped and compressed between layers of rock, breaks down slowly under pressure and heat into a dense organic material rich in humic substances. It's essentially the compressed by-product of ancient plant decay squeezed out of the mountainside.

Herbase's resin is described as dual-extracted and lab-tested, sold in a 50 g amber glass jar. Fulvic acid and humic acid are the two named compounds on the listing, both naturally occurring humic substances typical of this kind of material rather than anything unique to this product. The listing also names a longer list of minerals present, including zinc, copper, nickel, manganese, potassium, phosphorus, vanadium, chromium, cobalt and magnesium, though it doesn't give a lab-verified breakdown with quantities.

Because shilajit is scraped from rock rather than grown and harvested, purity testing is a real and useful thing to ask about, specifically testing for heavy metals like lead, arsenic and mercury, which can occur alongside the mineral content in unrefined material from some sources. Whether this particular resin has been tested for that isn't stated on the current listing, and it's the single fact that would most improve this page.
spec: Dual-extracted, lab-tested, as stated on the listing
Zinc, copper, nickel, manganese, potassium, phosphorus, vanadium, chromium, cobalt, magnesium, without stated quantities
Not stated on the current listing
dose: A pea-sized portion dissolved in 300 to 500 ml of warm spring water, taken once daily in the morning, or morning and evening.
supply: One 50 g jar. Printed on the listing as approximately a two month supply.
cautions: Always consult a healthcare professional before use.
Not for use in pregnancy or while breastfeeding without medical advice.
Material scraped directly from rock can carry heavy metals if it isn't properly tested and purified. Ask to see a certificate of analysis before use if you have any doubt.

body: Mycrodose combines four mushroom species in one capsule: Hericium erinaceus (lion's mane), Cordyceps militaris (cordyceps), Inonotus obliquus (chaga) and Ganoderma lucidum (reishi). Each is listed on the label as 100% pure, and the capsule shell itself is named as hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, a plant-derived vegan capsule material.

The pack is 50 capsules at 800 mg each. What isn't stated is how that 800 mg is divided between the four mushrooms, so we can't say how much of any single species is actually in a capsule. As with the single-species mushroom pages in this batch, the listing also doesn't say whether each mushroom is fruiting body or mycelium grown on grain, what extraction method is used, or what the beta-glucan content is, for the blend as a whole or for any of the four species individually.
